newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-No illusion, this magicians' feud is for real.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-No illusion, this magicians' feud is for real.

text.p: It's no illusion. Two of America's foremost magicians are locked in a bitter feud that has each wishing he could make the other disappear.

In a conjuring controversy, David Copperfield and Herbert Becker have sued each other over the two things most important in their world of smoke and mirrors: the secrets of their tricks and their credibility with audiences. No magic wand seems capable of easing their hurt feelings as Copperfield accuses Becker of a "malicious" and "vicious" vendetta and Becker calls his rival a crass publicity-seeker.

The bitter potion was mixed three weeks ago when Becker filed suit in Florida accusing Copperfield -- whose real name is David Seth Kotkin -- of causing a breach of contract between him and his publisher. For good measure, Becker's $50 million suit also names Lifetime Books, which published his "All the Secrets of Magic Revealed."

Faster than you can say "Abracadabra," Copperfield pulled his own legal rabbit from a hat, naming Becker in a $30 million defamation suit against Paris Match magazine. He said Becker was behind an article in the French publication that alleged Copperfield's romance with supermodel Claudia Schiffer was a sham.

In his suit filed in Los Angeles last week, Copperfield described Becker as "a failed magician, with a history of fraudulent behaviour, who is driven by envy and hatred to pursue an obsessive vendetta" against his rival.

Hey presto! Within hours, Becker shot back, charging that Copperfield was trying to divert attention from Becker's lawsuit by alleging Becker was the source for the story that Schiffer was playing Copperfield's fiancee for the publicity.
"David and Claudia have been caught in a major lie. Seems to me that Kotkin is trying to use some of his magical misdirection," Becker said.

The magician, who said he was headlining shows in the 1970s when Copperfield was still an up-and-coming conjurer, denied telling Paris Match about Schiffer but told Reuters he had seen a "contract" setting out the arrangement.
"He is not successful with women," Becker said of Copperfield. "I feel badly for him. He wants to be a star like Madonna, who the tabloids chase after, but he simply doesn't have the charisma."

He said Copperfield had approached him in 1993, when Becker was writing a book about the lives of great magicians and the secrets of some of their most famous tricks. Copperfield asked to be included in the book and the two worked together, Becker said, explaining the secrets behind some of Copperfield's illusions, among other things.

Later, Copperfield sued to stop publication, "accusing me of revealing how his tricks were done," Becker said. Copperfield lost that suit, but when the book was published in 1995 the sections on Copperfield's tricks had mysteriously disappeared, Becker said.
The publishers refused to explain to him why that happened but he believes his rival was involved, which is the basis of his breach-of-contract suit.

Copperfield, for his part, had no further comment except what he said in his latest suit, that it was untrue the German-born Schiffer was being paid to accompany him. "Mr. Copperfield and Ms. Schiffer met on the job, fell in love and plan to marry. They are not pretending to be anything to anyone," the suit said.
In addition to the $30 million in compensatory damages he is seeking, Copperfield asked for punitive damages against Becker, whom he described as "spiteful and vindictive."
So far there is no sign either suit will disappear soon in a puff of smoke. Meanwhile, it seems the two famous magicians would like to saw each other in half -- for real.
